title: Terbinafine and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Drink on Lamisil?
excerpt: Can you drink on terbinafine (Lamisil)? How the antifungal and alcohol affect your liver, tablets vs. cream, how long to wait, and the warning signs that need a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you drink on terbinafine (Lamisil)? How it and alcohol affect your liver over a 6-12 week course, tablets vs. cream, and warning signs to watch for.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** terbinafine (brand name Lamisil) does not cause a sudden, violent reaction with alcohol the way metronidazole can, and no study has shown that a drink makes the medicine work less well. The real issue is your liver. Oral terbinafine carries an official warning about rare but serious liver injury, and alcohol is processed by the same organ. Because a typical course for a nail infection runs 6 to 12 weeks, the question isn't really "can I have one drink?" It's "how much am I drinking across three months while my liver is handling a medicine that's known to strain it in rare cases?" Light, occasional drinking is generally considered low risk for a healthy adult. Regular heavy drinking during a course is a bad idea.

**The quick rules:** If you're using terbinafine **cream, gel, or spray** on your skin, alcohol isn't a meaningful concern, because very little of the drug gets into your bloodstream. If you're taking terbinafine **tablets**, keep drinking light and occasional for the whole course, skip binge nights, and tell your prescriber honestly how much you usually drink. Stop drinking and call your doctor promptly if you notice nausea that won't go away, loss of appetite, unusual tiredness, pain under your right ribs, dark urine, pale stools, or yellowing of your skin or eyes.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label information. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and your full medication list. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking on terbinafine if** you have liver disease or have ever had abnormal liver tests, you drink three or more drinks on most days, you take other prescription medicines (especially antidepressants or heart medicines), or you're pregnant or breastfeeding. **Get medical care promptly if** you develop persistent nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, unusual fatigue, pain in the upper right abdomen, dark urine, pale stools, or yellow skin or eyes while taking terbinafine or shortly after stopping. **Get emergency care** for a severe rash with blistering or peeling skin, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing. In an emergency, call 911.

## How Terbinafine and Alcohol Actually Interact

To understand the risk, it helps to know what terbinafine does and where your body sends it.

Terbinafine is an antifungal. It blocks an enzyme fungi need to build their cell membranes (the enzyme is called squalene epoxidase). Without it, the fungus can't maintain its outer wall and dies off. That's why it works well against the fungi that cause toenail and fingernail infections, ringworm, athlete's foot, and jock itch.

When you swallow a terbinafine tablet, your liver does most of the work of breaking it down. It uses several enzymes from the cytochrome P450 family to do that. Alcohol is also processed mainly in the liver, through a different set of enzymes (alcohol dehydrogenase and, in heavier drinkers, an enzyme called CYP2E1).

So here's the honest picture of how the two overlap:

1. **There is no known direct chemical clash.** Terbinafine doesn't block the enzyme that clears acetaldehyde, the toxic by-product of alcohol. That's the mechanism behind the flushing, pounding heart, and vomiting reaction you can get with metronidazole or disulfiram. Terbinafine doesn't do this, so a drink isn't going to make you suddenly sick.
2. **Both put demands on the liver.** Terbinafine can, rarely, cause liver injury on its own. Alcohol, especially in larger amounts, inflames and stresses liver cells. Doctors worry that stacking the two increases the chance of trouble, or makes trouble harder to spot.
3. **Their side effects overlap.** Terbinafine commonly causes stomach upset, nausea, diarrhea, and headache. Alcohol and hangovers cause the same things. That makes it harder to tell whether you're having a normal rough morning or an early sign of a drug reaction.
4. **Heavy drinking muddies your blood tests.** Your doctor may check your liver enzymes before or during treatment. Heavy drinking can raise those numbers by itself. If they come back high, nobody can easily tell whether the medicine or the alcohol is to blame, which can lead to stopping a treatment that was otherwise working.

The bottom line on mechanism: the risk isn't a dramatic reaction. It's added load and added confusion on an organ that's already doing extra work.

## The Liver Warning on Oral Terbinafine, Explained

If you read the patient leaflet that came with your tablets, you probably noticed the liver warning. Here's what it means in plain terms.

The US prescribing information for oral terbinafine states that cases of liver failure, some leading to liver transplant or death, have been reported in people taking it, including people with no history of liver disease. Because of that, the label says oral terbinafine isn't recommended for people with chronic or active liver disease, and it advises checking liver function with a blood test before starting treatment.

That sounds alarming, so let's put it in context.

- **Serious liver injury is rare.** The US National Institutes of Health's LiverTox database describes terbinafine liver injury as rare and idiosyncratic. "Idiosyncratic" means it's an unpredictable reaction in a small number of people, not a dose-related effect that builds up in everyone.
- **When it happens, it usually shows up within the first weeks.** LiverTox notes that reactions typically appear within the first several weeks of treatment, which is part of why doctors stress paying attention to symptoms early on.
- **It often starts quietly.** The early signs are easy to dismiss: feeling tired, not wanting to eat, mild nausea, itchy skin. Later, you may notice dark urine, pale stools, or yellowing of the eyes or skin.

Alcohol doesn't cause this idiosyncratic reaction, and there's no good evidence that a few drinks make it more likely. But if your liver is already inflamed from regular heavy drinking, it has less reserve to cope if a reaction does start. And the early warning signs of a terbinafine reaction look a lot like a hangover. Those are the two practical reasons to keep alcohol light during a course.

## Lamisil and Alcohol: Tablets vs. Cream

People searching "Lamisil and alcohol" are often asking about two very different products, so it's worth separating them.

### Lamisil tablets (oral terbinafine)

These are prescription tablets in the US, usually 250 mg once a day. They're mostly used for fungal nail infections, and sometimes for scalp ringworm or stubborn skin infections that haven't responded to creams. Everything in this article about the liver applies to the tablets.

### Lamisil cream, gel, and spray (topical terbinafine)

These are sold over the counter for athlete's foot, jock itch, and ringworm. When you rub terbinafine on your skin, only a tiny amount reaches your bloodstream. That means the liver concerns attached to the tablets don't really apply. Drinking a normal amount while using terbinafine cream is not considered a meaningful interaction.

A couple of practical notes on topical products:

- Some spray and solution versions contain alcohol as an ingredient. That's about evaporation and skin feel, not something that interacts with drinking.
- Heavy drinking can lead to sweating, poor sleep, and less attention to foot hygiene, none of which help a skin fungus clear up. That's a lifestyle point, not a drug interaction.

If you're not sure whether your product is oral or topical, look at the packaging or ask your pharmacist. A tablet you swallow and a cream you apply are treated very differently.

## How Long Does a Terbinafine Course Last?

The length of your course is a big part of why the alcohol question matters. Typical oral treatment lengths for adults are:

| Infection | Typical oral course |
|---|---|
| Fingernail fungus | About 6 weeks |
| Toenail fungus | About 12 weeks |
| Scalp ringworm and some skin infections | Varies, often a few weeks |

Your prescriber may adjust these, so follow their instructions. But for most people taking tablets, you're looking at one and a half to three months. That covers several weekends, probably a holiday or two, and maybe a wedding or a work event. Planning for that span is more useful than asking about a single drink.

It's also worth knowing that terbinafine is very fat-loving. It builds up in the skin, nails, and fatty tissue and leaves slowly. That's actually why it works: the drug keeps working in the nail for a while after you stop. It also means terbinafine is still present in your body for weeks after your last tablet, though at much lower levels than during treatment.

Don't expect your nails to look clear by the end of the course. Toenails grow slowly, and it can take many months after treatment for a healthy nail to grow out fully. Drinking more because "the treatment didn't work" isn't a sign anything went wrong. That's just how nails grow.

## Can You Drink Alcohol While Taking Terbinafine?

For most healthy adults without liver disease, light and occasional drinking during a terbinafine course is generally considered low risk. The safest choice is not drinking at all, and some doctors will recommend that, especially for longer courses. What's clearly a bad idea is heavy or daily drinking while on the tablets.

A practical way to think about it:

- **Lower concern:** a healthy adult with normal liver tests who has an occasional drink, stays within general moderation guidelines (US dietary guidelines describe moderate drinking as up to one drink a day for women and up to two for men, on days when people drink), and isn't taking other medicines that load the liver.
- **Ask first:** anyone who drinks most days, anyone who's had abnormal liver tests in the past, anyone on several other prescriptions, and anyone who isn't sure how much they actually drink in a typical week.
- **Avoid alcohol and talk to your doctor:** anyone with known liver disease, fatty liver, hepatitis, or a history of heavy drinking, and anyone who has started feeling unwell on terbinafine.

### Why binge nights are the bigger problem

Five or six drinks in one night puts a sharp load on your liver, upsets your stomach, and often leads to a rough next day with nausea and fatigue. On terbinafine, that next-day misery is exactly the cluster of symptoms you're supposed to watch for as a warning sign. A heavy night makes it hard to know what you're feeling and why. If you have a big event during your course, pace yourself, alternate with water, and eat a proper meal first.

### Does alcohol make terbinafine less effective?

There's no good evidence that alcohol stops terbinafine from killing the fungus. The concern is safety, not effectiveness. The one indirect way drinking can undermine treatment is if a hangover or a reaction leads you to skip doses or stop early. Nail infections need the full course to have the best chance of clearing.

## How Long After Terbinafine Can You Drink?

There's no official waiting period printed on the label for alcohol after terbinafine. Most people can return to their usual drinking after finishing the course, as long as they feel well.

Some sensible points:

- **Finish strong.** If you've been keeping alcohol light during treatment, there's no reason to celebrate the last tablet with a heavy night.
- **Liver reactions can show up late.** Problems usually appear within the first weeks, but it's wise to stay alert to symptoms like dark urine, yellow eyes, or persistent nausea for a few weeks after you stop, too.
- **If you had any liver issues during treatment,** ask your doctor before returning to regular drinking. They may want to recheck your blood tests first.
- **If you drink heavily,** the end of a course is a good moment to look honestly at how much. Your liver handles alcohol better when it isn't asked to process large amounts often.

## Side Effects That Overlap With Drinking

Most people take terbinafine without serious problems. The more common side effects, according to the label, include:

- Diarrhea, indigestion, nausea, and stomach pain
- Headache
- Rash and itching
- Changes in taste, and sometimes smell

A few of these are worth expanding on, because alcohol can make them worse or harder to read.

### Stomach upset

Terbinafine and alcohol can each irritate your gut. Together, especially on an empty stomach, you're more likely to end up with nausea or loose stools. Eating before you drink and staying hydrated helps.

### Taste and smell changes

Terbinafine can change how things taste, and in some people this lasts for weeks or longer after stopping. If drinks or food suddenly taste strange, metallic, or flat, the medicine may be the reason. Tell your doctor, because a lasting taste change can affect appetite and weight. Don't try to fix it with more alcohol or salty bar snacks.

### Mood changes

The terbinafine label lists depressive symptoms as a possible side effect. Alcohol is a depressant and can worsen low mood, especially the day after drinking. If you notice your mood dropping during a course, mention it to your prescriber and go easy on alcohol.

### Skin reactions

Rarely, terbinafine can cause serious skin reactions. A rash that blisters, peels, or comes with fever is an emergency. Don't assume it's from something you ate or drank.

## Terbinafine, Alcohol, and Other Medicines

This is where people get caught out. Terbinafine is a strong blocker of a liver enzyme called CYP2D6. That enzyme helps clear several common medicines, so terbinafine can raise their levels in your blood. Examples include:

- Some antidepressants, including older tricyclic antidepressants (such as nortriptyline) and some SSRIs
- Some beta blockers used for blood pressure and heart rhythm (such as metoprolol)
- Dextromethorphan, the cough suppressant in many cold medicines

Terbinafine can also slow how quickly your body clears caffeine, so your usual coffee may feel stronger.

Why does this matter for alcohol? Several of those medicines already carry their own alcohol warnings. If terbinafine raises their levels, the drowsiness, dizziness, or blood pressure effects of combining them with alcohol can get stronger too. If you take any of these, ask your pharmacist to check your full list before you drink during a course.

Two other combinations deserve a mention:

- **Acetaminophen (Tylenol).** Acetaminophen is a common painkiller and is also processed by the liver. A normal dose is generally fine, but heavy drinking plus regular acetaminophen plus terbinafine adds up. Our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the acetaminophen side in detail.
- **Other antifungals.** If you've also taken an oral antifungal like fluconazole recently, your liver has had extra work. Our [fluconazole and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/fluconazole-and-alcohol) covers that medicine's interaction pattern.

For a broader look at which prescriptions don't mix well with drinking, see our overview of [alcohol and medications](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications).

## Warning Signs: When to Stop and Call Your Doctor

Whether or not you've been drinking, these symptoms during or shortly after a terbinafine course mean you should stop the medicine and contact your doctor promptly. The label lists them as possible signs of liver problems:

- Nausea or vomiting that doesn't go away
- Loss of appetite
- Unusual tiredness or weakness
- Pain or discomfort in the upper right part of your abdomen
- Dark (tea- or cola-colored) urine
- Pale or clay-colored stools
- Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes

Here's the tricky part for social drinkers. Several of these look like a hangover. The difference is timing and persistence. A normal hangover fades as the day goes on and is usually gone within about 24 hours. Liver-related symptoms tend to hang around for days, get worse, or come with color changes in urine, stools, or eyes that a hangover doesn't cause. If you're not sure, assume it might be the medicine and call. Your doctor can order a simple blood test.

**Go to an emergency room or call 911 for:** a widespread rash with blistering or peeling, swelling of the lips, face, or throat, trouble breathing, confusion, or vomiting blood.

If you're worried about pain on your right side after drinking in general, our article on [liver pain after drinking](/never-hungover/liver-pain-after-drinking) explains what can cause it and when to get checked.

## Practical Tips If You Choose to Drink on Terbinafine

If you're a healthy adult, your doctor has said occasional drinking is fine, and you've decided to have a drink during your course, these habits keep the risk lower:

1. **Be honest with your prescriber up front.** Tell them roughly how many drinks you have in a typical week. It helps them decide whether to check your liver tests and how closely to watch.
2. **Keep it light and occasional.** One or two drinks on a night out is a very different picture from five or six, or a drink every night.
3. **Eat first.** Food slows alcohol absorption and eases stomach upset from both the drink and the medicine.
4. **Hydrate.** Alternate alcoholic drinks with water.
5. **Don't double up on liver-heavy medicines.** Avoid taking extra acetaminophen to manage a hangover unless you need it, and if you do, stick to a single standard dose.
6. **Don't skip doses.** If you've had a few drinks, take your next terbinafine dose as scheduled unless you feel unwell. Skipping doses doesn't "protect" your liver in any meaningful way and can make treatment less effective.
7. **Pay attention to how you feel.** If a "hangover" seems worse than normal or doesn't clear by the next day, take it seriously.
8. **Keep any blood test appointments.** If your doctor orders a recheck, go, and avoid heavy drinking for a few days beforehand so the result is clear.

## What About Supplements for Liver Support?

It's natural to wonder whether a liver supplement could balance things out while you're on terbinafine. Be careful here. There's no good evidence that any supplement protects against terbinafine liver injury, and some herbal products carry their own liver risks. Adding something new mid-course also makes it harder to know what's behind any reaction. Check with your pharmacist or prescriber before starting anything, and if you do get a liver reaction, mention every supplement you've taken.

Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known about combining DHM with prescription medicines, including how little human interaction data exists.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that some people take around drinking. Lab and animal studies suggest it may help the body process alcohol and may have protective effects on the liver, but human data is still limited. There's no good evidence that DHM protects against terbinafine liver injury, and it doesn't make heavy drinking safe during a course. If you're on oral terbinafine, the best liver protection is simply keeping alcohol light and following your doctor's advice.

Once you've finished your course and your doctor is happy with how you're doing, some people who drink socially choose to use DHM on nights out. If you're curious, two of the most-reviewed options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Ask your pharmacist before combining any supplement with prescription medicine, including terbinafine.

## The Bottom Line

Terbinafine and alcohol don't cause a dramatic reaction, and there's no good evidence that drinking makes the antifungal work less well. The real concern with the tablets is your liver: oral terbinafine carries an official warning about rare but serious liver injury, and alcohol adds to the liver's workload and makes early warning signs harder to spot. For a healthy adult, light and occasional drinking during a 6- to 12-week course is generally considered low risk. Heavy, daily, or binge drinking is not. Topical terbinafine creams and sprays don't raise these concerns. If you have liver disease, drink most days, or take other prescription medicines, talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking at all, and stop the medicine and call your doctor if you notice signs like dark urine, yellow eyes, or nausea that won't quit.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking terbinafine?**

For most healthy adults without liver disease, light and occasional drinking is generally considered low risk while taking terbinafine tablets. There's no dramatic reaction like the one metronidazole can cause. Heavy or daily drinking is a bad idea because oral terbinafine carries a warning about rare liver injury, and alcohol adds to the liver's workload. If you have liver disease or drink most days, ask your doctor first.

**Can I drink alcohol while using Lamisil cream?**

Yes, for most people. Very little terbinafine gets into your bloodstream when you apply it to your skin, so the liver concerns linked to the tablets don't really apply. Normal drinking while using terbinafine cream, gel, or spray isn't considered a meaningful interaction.

**How long after taking terbinafine can I drink alcohol?**

There's no official waiting period. Most people can return to their usual drinking once they finish the course and feel well. Stay alert for liver warning signs, like dark urine, yellow eyes, or ongoing nausea, for a few weeks after stopping, and check with your doctor first if you had any liver problems during treatment.

**Does alcohol stop terbinafine from working?**

There's no good evidence that alcohol makes terbinafine less effective against fungus. The concern is safety, not effectiveness. The main way drinking can undermine treatment is indirectly, if a hangover or side effects lead you to skip doses or stop the course early.

**Is terbinafine hard on the liver?**

For most people, no. Serious liver injury from terbinafine is rare. But it can happen, including in people with no prior liver disease, which is why the label recommends a liver blood test before starting and advises against oral terbinafine for people with chronic or active liver disease. Report symptoms like persistent nausea, fatigue, dark urine, or yellow skin or eyes right away.

**What are the signs of liver problems on terbinafine?**

Watch for nausea or vomiting that doesn't go away, loss of appetite, unusual tiredness, pain in the upper right abdomen, dark urine, pale stools, and yellowing of the skin or eyes. Some of these look like a hangover, but liver symptoms usually last for days and may come with color changes a hangover doesn't cause. Stop the medicine and call your doctor if you notice them.

**Can terbinafine interact with other medicines I take with alcohol?**

Yes. Terbinafine blocks a liver enzyme (CYP2D6) that clears several medicines, including some antidepressants, some beta blockers, and the cough suppressant dextromethorphan. Higher levels of those medicines can make their own alcohol effects, like drowsiness or dizziness, stronger. Ask your pharmacist to check your full medication list.

**Does DHM protect your liver while taking terbinafine?**

There's no good evidence that DHM protects against terbinafine liver injury, and it doesn't make heavy drinking safe during a course. DHM has early research on alcohol metabolism and liver health, mostly from animal studies. Ask your pharmacist before combining any supplement with prescription medicine.
